There are plenty of mods that require modification of both the server and the client software, e.g. if new items or game modes are added and the client needs to be able to recognize them. Even without any mods, there's a lot of trust required between the client and the server in pretty much any online game. text:
Well, after 15 years of saying "Someday I'll turn this into a web app," I finally did it!

I've been maintaining a popular repo of terminal themes at https://github.com/mbadolato/iTerm2-Color-Schemes, and it was finally time to build the app with all the features I wanted!

So, the next-gen version is live at https://terminalthemes.com! It currently has over 800 themes, and provides downloads for close to 40 different formats (iTerm, Ghostty, Windows, and many more)

It's free for everyone. An account is not needed to browse and download, but registering for an account (free) allows you to vote, bookmark, submit themes, etc.

I focused on a11y features for those who need it, in addition to adding Find My Theme and other tools to make it easy to find something you like!

Live terminal and code previews help show a more realistic view of the terminal, as opposed to the ANSI screenshots used at the GitHub repository. Those are still there, for those who like them.

I would love for you guys to check it out and provide feedback, feature suggestions, whatever!

And a huge thanks to the community of people that have contributed themes, ports to other terminals, and tools to provide conversions between formats over the years.

Oh! And if you've ever contributed themes to the GitHub repo, please register for an account, find your theme(s), and hit the Claim Authorship button!

(I treat patients at a cancer center, but opinions are my own and not those of my employer.)

I fully encourage any patient who wants another opinion to get one. Definitely really good advice to seek one out before you start on your treatment plan, if it can be done without undue delay. I think of planning cancer treatment like lining up to take off for a flight: some plans even if imperfect are more dangerous to alter than continue if they've already been put in motion. There are--rarely, thankfully--times where we don't end up concurring at all in the diagnosis or treatment, and this is all best sorted out before the first treatment.

But a second opinion isn't a waste just because it agrees with the initial plan. In my experience, that's actually the most common outcome, and I think it's a really good thing if a second opinion can give deserved reassurance that your original team is doing everything by the book. For many common cancers, there's consensus as to the most appropriate first-line treatment because there's peer-reviewed evidence and agreement on how to apply that evidence. When all of it points towards an effective treatment, down to a standardized dose and schedule, and it's a really good thing!

There's some subtlety that arises when there isn't a clear consensus as to which of (say) two reasonable approaches used by different comprehensive cancer centers is best. If you look at guidelines, both of those approaches would be listed as appropriate, but patients might be recommended one plan at center A and a different one at center B.

What it can come down to is that center A delivering treatment A demonstrates comparable results to center B delivering treatment B. In that scenario, if a patient lives down the street from center A and travels hundreds of miles to see me for a second opinion at center B, I would almost always agree with getting treatment A at center A. Not because I'm trying to manage what center A would think of me, but because I'd truly believe it's in that specific patient's best interest. First, all else being equal, I'd have no grounds to think that traveling hundreds of miles to get treatment B at center B would be better than staying local. Second, in general, I'd strongly doubt that getting treatment B at center A (which wouldn't be the plan they'd have the most experience with) would be superior to getting treatment A at center A.

And, yes, I absolutely have recommended when appropriate for patients to transfer care to our center, and I have also recommended when appropriate for patients to leave our center to go elsewhere (for example, for a particularly promising clinical trial option). I've seen every one of my colleagues do the same without hesitation.

This is all just from one person's perspective, of course. I know patients and families can come from different and totally valid vantage points. But to sum it up, please don't worry about managing your doctors' emotions about getting a second opinion, and find a place where you can be confident that the folks giving you their second opinion likewise aren't thinking about managing your doctors' emotions. Hopefully, they'll earn your trust that a concurring opinion means they really do think your original team has laid out the plan that's best for you.

title: Show HN: TowerPanic – a family party game on a small FastAPI realtime engine
text:
I want to show you the game I created recently and tell you whole the story/experience - including backend/latency/scalability.

You can try it quickly without an account - I created game demo rooms (EU/US/JP) - links below - just be aware that anyone with a link can access join the game.

Let's start with short description of the game itself:

This is the TowerPanic game - you are standing on one of four towers, during each round some of towers crack, and some of these lean, and finally one of these colapse - you need to watch out to not be on the failing one. It's a multiplayer game for whole family. This can be also used as an icebreaking game - for people in any age. The game is safe for children - no violence, no strangers, no chat, no ads. Parent creates an account (free 14-day trial, then a paid pass) and starts the game - others join using a QR code or a link.

Behind the game there is an interesting backend engine - I willdescribe it in a moment.

Let's start with the history of this whole project: - I was playing with asyncio and fastapi - As an exercise I created a reliable chat application (multiple rooms, in each room each user can reliably broadcast a message to all other users) - I extracted communication to separate layer - creating network/application layer interfaces - 'reliable client' interface for client and 'state machine' interface for the service on server. - With these interfaces - I was able to create other service - an 'sgame' (simple game). With verified interfaces and created services (chat, sgame) I was able to ask AI to generate other tools/games - I was impressed by these results - the games/tools worked well - I deployed them on a remote server - I was surprised that the latency was very good - almost everything worked smoothly

I tested the tools and games with my children and one of the game was really great. I decided to make this game public - I chose 'TowerPanic' name for it.

I prepared an account/payment server for this game (as a separate FastAPI application). This was very good choice: - the game servers keep rooms only in memory - nothing persistent (rooms have expiration date) - the account server keeps all persistent data (it uses database)

Because of this split I was able to figure out how to upgrade and scale frontend and backend independently - without significantly impacting users.

I optimized the communication layer - so that it works in finite memory - only finite number of recent messages is kept, and I sent a full service snapshot (full state) to the lagging clients.

The backend process (FastAPI/python) is limited by python GIL (only one core can be utilized) - to utilize all server cores I used HAProxy with consistent hashing to distribute rooms - so that users can be redirected to proper backend process.

I tested how many rooms a single server can handle - it handles hundreds of active rooms in parallel with no significant latency drop.

Before making it public I noticed that latency in other region of world might be higher and this could influence UX - I confirmed this using artificial delay on my remote server.

I decided to deploy the application in three regions - EU, US, JP - to ensure low latency (below 150ms) in most of the world. The room is created in region closest to the user (best latency from the browser to backend).

I needed also to prepare some legal documents (terms, privacy, refunds) - thanks to AI this was much easier. I'm a backend engineer, frontend/UI/UX were designed by me but code was generated by AI.

To summerize all this work: - I'm happy that I was able to deliver complete game/complete product - I think the whole work took me about 20 evenings - I'm impressed that it was so short - I think this is because the technology I used is popular and all fits well - AI was great as a peer (to discuss the options for distributing the load, discuss were to locate servers, or discuss how auth/payments work under the hood, ... - based on this I could choose the best option) - AI was great for doing the non work which I'm doing ineffectively (frontend/UI/legal docs).

That's not the argument being made.

The argument I'm making is that the only MITM/phishing vulnerability is in the initial passkey registration and not in the auth.

So once you have a passkey and the flow supports attestation, as long as you use the passkey you are effectively immune to MITM and phishing.

Now if you input a password or recovery code or whatever and use that to register a new passkey that's initial passkey registration again and not MITM or phishing of the passkey itself. The reason this matters is because you can register as many passkeys as you want. Say you sign up and log in on your phone. Now you register a passkey on the phone. You want to log in on your laptop, use the key from your phone to log in and register one for the laptop as well. Now you lose your phone or your laptop, you use the other to log you in and set up a new passkey for that device.

Once that initial passkey was registered the auth process is pretty watertight and each device you regularly use gets a new key after auth so you generally always have at least one device that you can use to get into your others.

Now of course if you only have one device and it gets destroyed or if all your devices are destroyed in a fire or flood or whatever then you have to go through the untrusted reset/re-registration flow but in all other scenarios you always default to the passkey-based "use another device you own" methods to register new keys.

TLDR: the point is that you very rarely ever do a true cred reset. The flow itself incentivizes multiple passkey auth methods such that bootstrapping new keys from an untrusted environment is rarely if ever required. This works best for "core services" like your email/google acct/apple acct/microsoft acct where you are generally expected to want access to them anywhere you do stuff so the passkey flow is best pared with SSO to increase the odds you've used the acct on at least one other device.

A few things I learned being the hospital for half of this year (this is mostly specific to the US):

- If insurance refuses to cover something, check your insurance site for something called an explanation of benefits for that charge, which should give a clear reason why it was denied. Sometimes though (way more often than it should be) the reason is completely wrong, or vague, or nonexistent, or is just hard to understand, in which case call the insurance and harass them daily until they either pay for it or give you a sane explanation.

- If you go through all of that and they still won't pay, get in contact with whoever made the charge (hospital, lab, doctor, etc), and tell them that your insurance refused to cover it, and that you need to negotiate the price down. This works sometimes. Even when it doesn't work, they can usually get you on some sort of payment plan so that your checking account doesn't go immediately dry.

- In general, get used to spending all your time on the phone calling insurance and doctors trying to get people to take you seriously. This is problematic obviously because you're SICK so generally you're not exactly in a state where you can do that. If you have any friends or family, see if you can enlist them to call people for you. Also, if you can get access to a social worker, sometimes they will be able to help you with calling insurance places and that kind of stuff. If you're inpatient, just ask your nurse for a social worker - at all the hospitals I was in, they had social workers on call for stuff like that.

- Write down on your phone somewhere a bullet list of all of your symptoms, treatments, diagnosis (or attempted diagnoses), etc. You will constantly (and I mean CONSTANTLY) have doctors entering your room who have not even GLANCED at your chart, who have absolutely no idea what's going on, and who will seemingly make all of their decisions based on your answer to the question "so what's going on". So make sure you have a good answer to that, which makes it clear to them that you have a serious problem that is worth taking seriously.

- Adding to that, push each new doctor that comes in for an actual PLAN. Your doctors likely WILL NOT communicate and plan with each other -- treat yourself as the project manager. You are the go-between for everybody. If the neurologist says something, then next time you see the oncologist, make sure they know that the neurologist said that. It is unfortunately your responsibility to lead the team of doctors that cares for you, at least in my experience at a few different hospitals.

- If you have pain, don't be afraid to ask for pain meds, because unless you ask for them, they won't be given to you. Even if you're writhing and moaning in pain, you will either be ignored or given extra-strength tylenol. You have to constantly advocate for yourself and be persistent about getting actual pain medication. Even when they do give you opiates, they will try to give you the smallest possible oral dose unless you specifically tell them "I need this much of this kind, and I need it IV, otherwise it doesn't help enough".

- This includes learning how to use the 0-10 pain scale. If you're like me, your instinct will be to always undershoot your pain number, because yes this is excruciating but I'm sure people who've had full body chemical burns feel far worse than this, so maybe in the grand scheme of things what I'm feeling is just a 5 -- don't do that. The 0-10 pain scale, in practice, is actually a metric of "how much do I need pain medication right now". In my experience, anything from 0-5, even if it really hurts, will not get you real pain medication. 6-7 is like "wow this hurts, it would be nice to get something for the pain", and 8+ is "this is excruciating, I need pain medication right now".

Anyways, good article and I agree with everything there, especially the part about going to a major cancer center instead of your local hospital whenever possible. Just wanted to add some more thoughts from my own experience.

Hello! I am a practising dentist in Australia. I've been reading the comments and thought I'd add my own 2 cents in.

First, I think the reason for such variance in dentists' treatment planning is because of an increased clinical scope. I assume that the medical field is more hierarchal, so you increase your scope as you go along. For dentists, as soon as you graduate, you have an enormous scope as it's really dependent on your training and confidence in that procedure (obviously, overconfidence is akin to malpractice).

Why do some dentists overtreat? I think dentists fall into the bias of "if you have a hammer everything is a nail". Each dentist will have a preference for a specific treatment, but it's important at the end of the day for the treatment to align with the patient's objective. For example, a simple tooth replacement has so much options - dental implant, a 2-unit or 3-unit bridge, a Maryland/resin bonded bridge, a denture, or just do nothing! Each one has their pros and cons, and there is a risk where what the dentist thinks is ideal is not what the patient wants.

In terms of overdiagnosing cavities, I think it may arise from the dentists' training. Maybe in the past, any signs of decay indicated surgical drilling. However, modern training reinforces MID - minimally invasive dentistry - so we are taught to avoid drilling any decay that is confined to enamel.

Finally, I think dentists avoid throwing each other under the bus simply due to empathy. Working in a mouth is not easy, and each procedure comes with challenges. You're fighting against visibility - keeping the mouth open wide enough to see what you're doing; batting away saliva; constantly wiping your mirror from the handpiece water. Then you've got the gaggers, the anaesthetic doesn't work, etc etc. We will never know what someone else was going through in the moment of the procedure.

Both of these things are actually true. (I actually argue in the top comment that the positional information is the #1 reason why attention works, so I agree with this.)

Let's see why.

What are Q and K? The idea in the original paper was: we have some learned embeddings for our tokens, and some "context" we'd like to use to enrich those embeddings. Stuff like the positional information, context accumulated through layers, other learned stuff. So we do this enrichment, and that produces the so-called "query" (Q) and a "key" (K) vectors. Attention is STILL a weighted average, where the weights are determined by how "similar" those vectors are (this is what we're talking about when we discuss the "distance" provided by the so-called "kernel function").

Anyway the reason it's hard for me to parse this reply is because I think a lot is getting lost in the transition from a second language to English. For example, "distance" in this context means something specific, and to be precise the exponential kernel provides a similarity measurement (dot product can encode distance but generally requires fixed-length norms). The quiet part needs to be said out loud: ensuring "fairness" in online games and letting clients meaningfully remain in control over their hardware and software are two fundamentally incompatible goals. One goal puts the interests of the game publisher and community first, the other upholds the individual clients' interests.

Ideally there should be little conflict between the two, however, modern online games require running sophisticated software locally that encapsulates core game logic. The fairness (compliance) goal demands that this software runs correctly and only conveys information and processes input as designed. The user control (freedom) goal demands that the individual user is allowed to run and modify any software as they see fit, including any game software, meaning that he or she must be able to tamper with the game software behaviour to gain advantage.

Now remember that online gaming is an extremely low-trust environment. Competitive online gaming is often supposed to emulate sportsmanship, thus widespread trust in the games' rules is essential so that players continue to participate. At the same time, building that trust dictates enforcing compliance down to the level of each individual user's hardware. So if you want to participate, you must be willing to give up ultimate control over your hardware and software, even if you believe it's only temporary.

All of this might sound very obvious, tautological even. However, lots of comments on this sound like they come from a place of unawareness of this contradiction. More people need to see that this is not a tech incompatibility issue, but rather a more serious values clash. Linux folks are (still) mostly the ones who prefer more freedom and control over their software, and competitive online gaming asks that they give that up. For a lot of people this defeats the purpose of using Linux in the first place.

> Rust is managed by the Rust Foundation...

Sure, but that's the case for a lot of languages. ANSI X3.159-1989 (aka C89) shows that just about everyone involved was a representative for some big org, almost all commercial or military.

But if the foundation seems like it's mismanaging Rust, the community should feel free to fork it. The trademark isn't super important at the end of the day, it's the community. And the community is very well represented in the Rust Foundation by design AFAICT.

> There is a certain “social momentum” when it comes to the spread of Rust...

People like it, and it excites/inspires them to use it. And it's more than just memory safety. I commonly use it in deeply embedded cases where I'm doing silly stuff like 'unsafe fn main()'. The memory safety isn't the main draw for me. It's mostly the algebraic types, and the abstraction mechanism that's less interested in hiding data/code relationships than c++ is. The borrow checker is just a cherry on top.

That being said, I wouldn't confuse people's excitement for requirements on others. New code should have to make a case for itself on its own merits.

> One of the Rust community’s main passtimes, a meme at this point, is rewriting existing projects into Rust....

I would strongly encourage more rewriting projects.

What I would discourage is them being widely deployed. I do think Canonical jumped the gun a bit on their Rust adoption with sudo-rs and uutils.

> I believe this culture of rewriting existing projects benefits corporations (again).

This is hardly a Rust thing, and I think more on the ebb and flow of the era with new coders not understanding the purpose of the GPL and thinking that MIT/BSD licenses must mean more free rather than the rather nuanced discussions that can be in favor of either. We are starting to see push back on this though thankfully.

I am curious what the state of this looks like in a couple years given the recent bout of borderline forcible open source rewrites via coding agents.

> It’s completely possible that Rust’s compiler contains a backdoor.

This is practically a non issue; there are people who bootstrap Rust from source.

I would also throw out there that we'll probably see agents sifting through binaries before too long. They'll just be looking for exploitable bugs like the current explosion in LLM found security issues.

I would like to see other compilers though.

I actually do disagree with much the more explicit content of your comment, but I am not going to bother to expand on that, because it is the less directly relevant of the two disagreements here, and it would take time to write that.

The more relevant disagreement is that you are (I gather) assuming a context where justice and restitution are a sufficient response to the problem (or else you wouldn't be focusing on them to this extent, I am inferring). Like, where the incidents don't get that much bigger than what has already happened. So the question becomes how do we distribute the loss, and how do we disincentivize them.

However, when the scale of a potential incident gets big enough, justice and deterrence are not sufficient; prevention becomes the far more relevant consideration. You may have noticed that many people are worried about potential human extinction as a result of AIs. In that case, prevention becomes the only consideration -- justice is useless.

So there seems to be an implicit disagreement here between thinking of such events as being on a scale not too much larger than that which has already happened, being a new normal that the legal system will need to handle, vs thinking of such events as warning shots for something that requires prevention and not justice.

So, while I also disagree with the more explicit content of your comment, the fact is I simply wasn't thinking about such matters in the first place -- I was talking about this in the frame of a problem that requires prevention, I wasn't thinking about the justice question at all. It honestly failed to occur to me that you might be thinking of this as a problem where justice suffices!

And that is false, exactly because of that standard. If you want reproducible builds then you can stick with a previously built version of uv-build for a long time. If you want working builds on the fly using your own processes, then the standard empowers you to substitute something else. If you want to use the Python packaging ecosystem in the normal way, then it doesn't even matter what your distro is.

uv-build is for pure Python projects, which entails that the "build" process is trivial. It doesn't even bytecode-compile the .pyc files generally; wheels aren't expected to contain them (your installer may produce them at install time, or you can let Python produce them on demand). Binary reproducibility for pure-Python wheels is just not, from anything I've seen, a high priority for Python packaging.

Linux distros have these ideas about packaging that are just not suitable for Python and not in tune with what the Python ecosystem is doing. The vast majority of the Python code you install should not be integrated into your "system". (Python devs rarely find themselves wanting to "bootstrap" everything from source, either.) Gentoo's issue here appears to be their own policy, which is a problem of their own making. It's unrealistic for them to expect random Python devs to care about this.

> As the project developer, sure. But as a Linux distro building your python package, Gentoo has to use the build backend you specify. It can't say, well, this particular package is just pure python, so really all we need is a minimal tool to build a pure python none-any wheel. It has to use the backend you specified.

If you mean because of Gentoo policy, that's their fault. I can guarantee you that approximately nobody using uv-build is concerned with whether their package makes it into Portage. Python build systems aren't designed to produce packages native to Portage (or any other Linux packaging system). Probably the overwhelming majority of these users aren't expecting any Linux distro repositories to host their package in any form, and probably most of them couldn't even tell you what Gentoo is.

If you mean technically, then no; once you have the source code and are using ebuild, nothing compels you to choose the backend specified in pyproject.toml. If everything is up to standard then it's trivial to switch it over to, say, Flit. Most projects following a standard src layout will need no tool-specific config, and there's quite little of it possible regardless (and all well documented). The author even highlights:

> It’s a backend and the whole point of PEP 517 is that you can use any backend with any tool. You can use flit-core, you can use hatchling, and either of them will work just fine with uv (or any other frontend).

The edits do take time but it's a lot better than the proposed bogeyman of waiting for a new build of uv-build from Rust source.
